title: AP Chemistry
summary: Use particle models, quantitative reactions, equilibrium and energy reasoning.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Nine-unit map verified at https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-chemistry after the AP Students page timed out. Uses the Fall 2024 framework titles and boundaries; text exercises do not replace laboratory work.

modules.title: Atomic masses and electron attraction
modules.focus: Relate isotope composition to an average mass.
explanation: Isotopes of an element share a proton count but differ in neutron count. The periodic-table atomic mass is an abundance-weighted average, not necessarily the mass of any individual atom. Convert percentage abundances to fractions before weighting.

Electron attraction reflects nuclear charge, distance and shielding. Across a period, increasing effective nuclear attraction often decreases atomic radius. Ionisation-energy trends have exceptions tied to subshell occupancy and electron pairing, so a trend is a reasoned model rather than a substitute for structure.

workedExample.prompt: An element has isotopes of mass 10 u and 11 u with abundances 20% and 80%. Find its average mass.
steps: Weight the first isotope: 10(0.20)=2 u.
Add the second contribution 11(0.80)=8.8 u to obtain 10.8 u.

misconception.claim: Every atom has the decimal mass printed on the periodic table.
misconception.correction: That value averages isotopic masses across a sample.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 75% mass-35 and 25% mass-37 isotopes. Find the weighted mass.
questions.hint: Multiply each mass by its fraction.

questions.prompt: Why is a sodium ion smaller than a sodium atom?
questions.hint: Consider which shell loses an electron.
questions.answer: Na⁺ loses its outer-shell electron, leaving a smaller occupied-shell arrangement.
checkpoints: Do not describe a change in proton count.

questions.hint: Turn the ratio into fractions of the total.
questions.prompt: Isotopes of masses 20 u and 22 u occur in a 3:1 ratio. Find the average mass.
hints: Turn the ratio into fractions of the total.
Multiply each mass by its fraction.

questions.hint: Count electrons after each charge change.
questions.prompt: Rank the radii of O²⁻, F⁻ and Na⁺ from largest to smallest, explaining your control variable.
questions.answer: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺. Each has ten electrons; increasing proton number pulls that same electron configuration inward.
checkpoints: Identify all three as ten-electron ions.
Use stronger attraction to justify the radius order.
hints: Count electrons after each charge change.
Hold the electron arrangement fixed while comparing proton number.

notes.title: Reasoning through atomic masses and electron attraction
paragraphs: Isotopic abundance describes a population, so the mass on a periodic table is a weighted mean rather than the mass of one atom. Convert percentages to fractions before multiplying and check that their sum is one. Electron attraction depends on nuclear charge, shielding and distance; a simple claim that more protons always means a smaller atom ignores electron shells. Across one period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally pulls the same outer shell inward. When comparing isoelectronic ions, their electron arrangements match, so the ion with more protons generally has the smaller radius.

workedExamples.prompt: An element has isotopes of masses 62 u and 64 u. Its average mass is 62.6 u. Find each abundance.
steps: Let x be the fraction of mass-64: 62(1−x)+64x=62.6.
Then 2x=0.6, so x=0.30; the mass-62 fraction is 0.70.
workedExamples.conclusion: The sample is 70% mass-62 and 30% mass-64.

flashcards.front: What does a weighted atomic mass represent?
flashcards.back: The mean mass across the sample isotope population.

flashcards.front: What must isotope fractions sum to?
flashcards.back: One.

flashcards.front: What is shielding?
flashcards.back: Inner electrons reduce the attraction an outer electron experiences from the nucleus.

flashcards.front: Among isoelectronic Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, which is smaller?
flashcards.back: Mg²⁺, because its larger nuclear charge attracts the same electron count more strongly.

modules.title: Molecular geometry and polarity
modules.focus: Combine bond directions with bond dipoles.
explanation: A Lewis structure accounts for valence electrons and bonding. Electron-domain repulsion predicts arrangements around a central atom, counting a multiple bond as one domain. Lone pairs occupy domains and can change molecular shape and bond angles.

A polar bond does not guarantee a polar molecule. Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles and the spatial arrangement. Symmetric cancellation can produce a nonpolar molecule containing polar bonds.

workedExample.prompt: Compare the molecular polarity of linear CO₂ and bent H₂O.
steps: CO₂ has two opposing C-O bond dipoles that cancel in its linear geometry.
H₂O is bent, so its O-H dipoles do not cancel and the molecule has a net dipole.

misconception.claim: Any molecule containing polar bonds is polar.
misconception.correction: Geometry determines whether the bond dipoles cancel.

questions.prompt: How many electron domains surround carbon in CH₄, and what is its shape?
questions.answer: Four domains; tetrahedral shape.
checkpoints: There are no central lone pairs.
Use domain arrangement to identify shape.

questions.prompt: Why does a double bond count as one VSEPR domain?
questions.hint: A domain is a region of electron density.
questions.answer: Its electron density occupies one direction between the same two atoms.
checkpoints: Count regions, not individual electron pairs.
Keep bond order separate from domain count.

questions.prompt: For BF₃ with no lone pairs on B, identify domain count, shape and polarity.
questions.answer: Three domains, trigonal planar geometry, and a nonpolar molecule because the three identical B−F bond dipoles cancel.
hints: Count bonding regions around B.
Add the three equal bond dipoles as vectors.

questions.prompt: CH₃Cl has a tetrahedral central carbon. Does tetrahedral geometry guarantee a nonpolar molecule? Explain.
questions.answer: No. The substituents are unequal, so the C−Cl and C−H bond dipoles do not cancel; CH₃Cl is polar.
checkpoints: Connect incomplete dipole cancellation to polarity.
hints: Compare the four substituents.
A geometric shape must be combined with bond identities.

notes.title: Reasoning through molecular geometry and polarity
paragraphs: A Lewis structure counts valence electrons, while a VSEPR model organises regions of electron density around a central atom. Multiple bonds form one region each. First identify the electron-domain geometry, then describe the positions of atoms to name the molecular geometry; lone pairs occupy domains even though they are not atoms in the shape name. Molecular polarity is a vector result. Polar bonds can cancel in a symmetric arrangement, but unequal surrounding atoms or lone-pair-driven asymmetry can prevent cancellation. A flat drawing alone does not establish the three-dimensional bond-dipole sum.

workedExamples.prompt: Predict the molecular shape and polarity of NH₃, using its central nitrogen.
steps: N contributes five valence electrons and forms three N−H bonds, leaving one lone pair: four electron domains.
The domains are approximately tetrahedral, but the atoms form a trigonal pyramid; the bond dipoles do not cancel.
workedExamples.conclusion: NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal and polar.

flashcards.front: What does a lone pair contribute to VSEPR?
flashcards.back: One electron domain.

flashcards.front: How many domains does a triple bond occupy?
flashcards.back: One.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes molecular and electron geometry?
flashcards.back: Molecular geometry names atom positions; electron geometry includes lone-pair domains.

flashcards.front: Why is BF₃ nonpolar in its ideal geometry?
flashcards.back: Its three identical bond dipoles cancel in a trigonal plane.

modules.title: Intermolecular forces and solution concentration
modules.focus: Use particle interactions to explain bulk properties.
explanation: Intermolecular attractions influence boiling point, viscosity and solubility. London dispersion forces occur in all particles, while permanent dipoles and hydrogen bonding add other interactions when molecular structure permits. Boiling separates particles without normally breaking their covalent bonds.

Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. During dilution, solute amount stays constant if none reacts or is lost, so M₁V₁=M₂V₂. Use solution volume rather than assuming the solvent volume equals the final volume.

workedExample.prompt: What volume of 2.0 M stock is needed to prepare 250 mL of 0.40 M solution?
steps: Conserve solute: V₁=(0.40)(250)/2.0 mL.
Use 50 mL of stock and dilute to a final volume of 250 mL.

misconception.claim: Boiling water breaks its O-H covalent bonds.
misconception.correction: It primarily overcomes attractions between water molecules.

questions.prompt: Find molarity for 0.30 mol solute in 0.50 L solution.
questions.answer: 0.60 mol/L.

questions.prompt: Why can larger nonpolar molecules often have higher boiling points?
questions.answer: Their more polarisable electron clouds can produce stronger dispersion attractions.
checkpoints: Do not invent hydrogen bonding in a nonpolar hydrocarbon.

questions.prompt: How many grams of NaCl, molar mass 58.5 g/mol, are needed for 0.200 L of 0.50 M solution?
checkpoints: Use final solution volume in litres.
hints: Find moles using cV.
Convert moles to mass with the molar mass.

questions.prompt: Methane and methanol are both molecular substances. Explain why methanol has much stronger attractions between its molecules.
questions.answer: Both have dispersion forces. Methanol is polar and its O−H groups enable hydrogen bonding, while methane has no comparable permanent dipole or hydrogen-bond network.
checkpoints: Identify methanol hydrogen bonding and polarity.
Contrast methane without claiming that its attractions are absent.
hints: Look for an O−H bond.
Distinguish stronger attractions from no attractions.

notes.title: Reasoning through intermolecular forces and solution concentration
paragraphs: Intermolecular attractions affect physical properties without changing the covalent identity of individual molecules. London dispersion occurs in all atoms and molecules; polar molecules can also have permanent dipole interactions, and suitable N−H, O−H or F−H donors can hydrogen-bond with appropriate acceptors. Stronger attractions generally raise boiling temperature when other structural features are comparable. Concentration questions require a different distinction: molarity uses total solution volume, not solvent volume. Dilution conserves the amount of solute if none reacts or is lost, so the new volume includes both stock solution and added solvent.

workedExamples.prompt: Combine 100 mL of 0.20 M NaCl with 200 mL of 0.10 M NaCl. Assume additive volumes. Find the final concentration.
steps: The amounts are (0.100 L)(0.20 mol/L)=0.020 mol and (0.200 L)(0.10 mol/L)=0.020 mol.
Total amount is 0.040 mol in 0.300 L, giving 0.133 mol/L.
workedExamples.conclusion: The mixed solution is approximately 0.13 M NaCl.

flashcards.front: Which attraction occurs in every molecular substance?
flashcards.back: London dispersion.

flashcards.front: Why does dilution reduce molarity?
flashcards.back: The same solute amount occupies a larger solution volume.

flashcards.front: What volume belongs in n/V?
flashcards.back: Total solution volume in litres.

flashcards.front: Can ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to one another?
flashcards.back: Yes; their O−H groups can donate and oxygen lone pairs can accept.

modules.title: Stoichiometry and limiting reactants
modules.focus: Use balanced coefficients as mole ratios.
explanation: A balanced chemical equation conserves each element and charge. Its coefficients compare amounts in moles, not masses in grams. Convert measured masses to moles before applying the ratio, then convert back to a requested mass if needed.

A limiting reactant is consumed first under the reaction model and determines theoretical yield. Excess reactant remains. Actual yield may be lower because of incomplete conversion, competing reactions or product loss; percentage yield compares actual and theoretical amounts.

workedExample.prompt: For N₂+3H₂→2NH₃, combine 2 mol N₂ with 3 mol H₂. Find the theoretical ammonia amount.
steps: 3 mol H₂ can react with only 1 mol N₂, so hydrogen limits the reaction.
The ratio 3 H₂:2 NH₃ gives 2 mol NH₃, leaving 1 mol N₂.

misconception.claim: The reactant with fewer moles must be limiting.
misconception.correction: Compare available amounts with the balanced reaction ratio.

questions.prompt: For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, how much water forms from 5 mol H₂ and excess oxygen?
questions.answer: 5 mol H₂O.
checkpoints: Oxygen is stated to be in excess.

questions.prompt: Actual yield is 8 g and theoretical yield is 10 g. Find percentage yield.

questions.hint: Compare each amount divided by its coefficient.
questions.prompt: For 2CO+O₂→2CO₂, mix 3.0 mol CO with 2.0 mol O₂. Find CO₂ yield and remaining oxygen.
questions.answer: 3.0 mol CO₂ forms; 1.5 mol O₂ is consumed and 0.5 mol O₂ remains.
hints: Compare each amount divided by its coefficient.
Use the limiting amount to find oxygen consumption.

questions.prompt: A synthesis has theoretical yield 12.0 g but gives 9.0 g dry product. Calculate yield and explain why this alone does not identify the loss mechanism.
questions.answer: Yield is 75%. Several causes, including incomplete reaction, side reactions or transfer losses, could give the same recovered mass; further evidence is needed.
checkpoints: Name a plausible specific loss mechanism.
Explain why yield alone cannot distinguish mechanisms.
hints: Compare actual with theoretical mass.
Consider both chemical conversion and physical recovery.

notes.title: Reasoning through stoichiometry and limiting reactants
paragraphs: A balanced equation gives ratios between amounts in moles. It does not compare masses directly, so convert each reactant mass before deciding what limits the reaction. Dividing each available amount by its coefficient gives the number of reaction units it can support; the smallest value identifies the limiting reactant. Theoretical yield assumes that reactant follows the stated equation completely. Actual isolated yield can be lower because of incomplete conversion, competing reactions or material lost during separation. Excess reactant remains after the limiting reactant is consumed and must be calculated from the amount that actually reacts.

workedExamples.prompt: For 2Al+3Cl₂→2AlCl₃, mix 0.60 mol Al and 0.60 mol Cl₂. Find product and excess reactant.
steps: Compare 0.60/2=0.30 reaction units for Al with 0.60/3=0.20 for Cl₂; chlorine limits.
Product is 2(0.20)=0.40 mol AlCl₃; Al consumed is 0.40 mol, leaving 0.20 mol.
workedExamples.conclusion: Theoretical yield is 0.40 mol AlCl₃ and 0.20 mol Al remains.

flashcards.front: Why balance before calculating yield?
flashcards.back: Coefficients supply the conserved mole ratios.

flashcards.front: How is the limiting reactant identified?
flashcards.back: Compare available moles divided by each coefficient.

flashcards.front: Does excess mean all of a reactant remains?
flashcards.back: No; some reacts and the unused remainder is excess.

flashcards.front: What is percentage yield?
flashcards.back: Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100%.

modules.title: Rate laws from controlled comparisons
explanation: A rate law relates reaction rate to concentrations through experimentally determined exponents. These exponents cannot generally be read from the balanced overall equation. Hold other reactant concentrations constant when comparing the effect of one concentration.

Temperature can change the rate constant by changing the fraction of collisions able to cross an activation barrier. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway; it does not change the net stoichiometry or equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.

workedExample.prompt: Doubling [A] at fixed [B] quadruples rate. Doubling [B] at fixed [A] doubles rate. Find the rate law.
steps: For A, 2^m=4 gives m=2; for B, 2^n=2 gives n=1.
The rate law is rate=k[A]²[B].

misconception.claim: Overall equation coefficients always equal rate-law exponents.
misconception.correction: That inference requires an elementary-step model, not merely a balanced overall equation.

questions.prompt: For rate=k[A]², what happens to rate when [A] triples?
questions.answer: It increases by a factor of 9.

questions.prompt: A first-order process has half-life 6 minutes. What fraction remains after 18 minutes?

questions.hint: A concentration raised to zero contributes a factor of one.
questions.prompt: Doubling [A] at fixed conditions leaves rate unchanged. Tripling [B] at fixed [A] triples rate. Write the rate law.
questions.answer: rate=k[B]; the order in A is zero and the order in B is one.
hints: A concentration raised to zero contributes a factor of one.
Match the observed factor of three for B.

questions.hint: Apply the exponent to the concentration factor.
questions.prompt: A reaction has rate=k[A]². If [A] halves while temperature is fixed, find the new rate as a fraction of the old and explain why k is unchanged in this model.
questions.answer: The rate becomes one quarter. The concentration changes the [A]² factor; under the stated unchanged temperature and pathway, k is constant.
checkpoints: State the fixed-temperature and pathway assumption.
hints: Apply the exponent to the concentration factor.
Separate parameters of the rate law from changing reactant amounts.

notes.title: Reasoning through rate laws from controlled comparisons
paragraphs: A rate law connects measured rate to reactant concentrations under specified conditions. Overall balanced coefficients do not usually reveal experimental reaction orders. Compare two trials that change only one concentration, divide their rates and solve for the exponent. Once orders are known, substitute one complete trial to obtain the rate constant, retaining units that make the rate units consistent. The constant depends on temperature and on the pathway. A catalyst supplies a different pathway with a lower activation barrier, but does not change the equilibrium constant or the thermodynamic difference between products and reactants.

workedExamples.prompt: For rate=k[A][B]², a trial has [A]=0.20 M, [B]=0.50 M and rate=0.010 M/s. Find k and rate when B doubles.
steps: Doubling B with A fixed multiplies rate by 2²=4, giving 0.040 M/s.
workedExamples.conclusion: k is 0.20 M⁻² s⁻¹ and the new rate is 0.040 M/s.

flashcards.front: What controls experimental reaction order?
flashcards.back: The measured concentration dependence of rate.

flashcards.front: Can overall equation coefficients determine every rate law?
flashcards.back: No; only an elementary-step model permits direct molecularity reasoning.

flashcards.front: What is the overall order of k[A][B]²?
flashcards.back: Three.

flashcards.front: What does a catalyst change?
flashcards.back: The pathway and reaction rate, without changing K at fixed temperature.

modules.title: Calorimetry and energy accounting
modules.focus: Define the system before assigning a heat sign.
explanation: Heat transfer changes a material’s temperature according to q=mcΔT when the specific heat is approximately constant and no phase change occurs. A positive q means that the named system gains heat. Energy lost by one part must be gained elsewhere in an appropriately isolated model.

In a solution calorimeter, the measured solution warming usually indicates an exothermic reaction. The reaction heat has the opposite sign to the heat absorbed by solution and apparatus. Ignoring apparatus heat capacity is an approximation that should be stated.

workedExample.prompt: 100 g of water warms by 5.0°C. Use c=4.18 J/(g°C) to find heat absorbed.
steps: If only a reaction supplies that heat and apparatus absorption is neglected, the reaction releases 2.09 kJ.

misconception.claim: A temperature increase always means the reaction absorbed heat.
misconception.correction: The solution may warm because the reaction released heat to it.

questions.prompt: Find q for 50 g water cooling by 4°C with c=4.18 J/(g°C).
questions.answer: -836 J for the water.

questions.prompt: If a reaction releases 120 kJ per mole, what heat is associated with 0.25 mol reacting?
questions.answer: -30 kJ for the reaction.

questions.hint: Hess’s law adds equations and their enthalpy changes.
questions.prompt: Given A→B has ΔH=+25 kJ/mol and B→C has ΔH=−60 kJ/mol, find ΔH for A→C.
questions.answer: −35 kJ/mol, from 25−60 with intermediate B cancelled.
checkpoints: Add the reactions and cancel B.
hints: Hess’s law adds equations and their enthalpy changes.
Track signs before adding.

questions.prompt: A student ignores heat absorbed by a calorimeter during an exothermic reaction. What happens to the inferred magnitude of reaction heat if solution heat is measured correctly?
questions.answer: It is underestimated: the released energy heated both solution and calorimeter, but the calculation counted only the solution contribution.
checkpoints: Identify positive heat gained by the apparatus.
Include both gains in the energy balance.
Conclude the exothermic heat magnitude was underestimated.
hints: List everything that warmed.
Compare the counted heat with the full energy transfer.

notes.title: Reasoning through calorimetry and energy accounting
paragraphs: Choose the system before attaching a sign to heat. In a simple insulated coffee-cup model, heat gained by solution balances heat lost by the reacting chemicals; a calorimeter correction is needed if the apparatus absorbs appreciable heat. Use the temperature change of the material whose mass and specific heat appear in q=mcΔT. At constant pressure, reaction heat is related to enthalpy change for the amount that reacts. Hess’s law works because enthalpy is a state function: reverse an equation and reverse its enthalpy sign; multiply the equation and multiply its enthalpy by the same factor.

workedExamples.prompt: A reaction warms 200 g of solution from 20.0°C to 23.0°C. Use c=4.0 J/(g°C), negligible apparatus heat and 0.050 mol reacted. Find molar reaction enthalpy.
steps: Solution heat is 200×4.0×3.0=2400 J=2.4 kJ gained.
Reaction heat is −2.4 kJ, so ΔH=(−2.4)/0.050=−48 kJ/mol.
workedExamples.conclusion: The reaction enthalpy is −48 kJ/mol under the stated model.

flashcards.front: What sign does q have for a warming solution?
flashcards.back: Positive.

flashcards.front: Why is reaction heat opposite to solution heat here?
flashcards.back: Energy conservation in the assumed insulated two-part system.

flashcards.front: What happens to ΔH when an equation reverses?
flashcards.back: Its sign reverses.

flashcards.front: What happens to ΔH when coefficients double?
flashcards.back: It doubles.

modules.title: Equilibrium quotients and reaction direction
modules.focus: Compare the present composition with the equilibrium ratio.
explanation: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal while reactions continue microscopically. The equilibrium constant expresses a ratio of activities; introductory concentration expressions approximate this using suitable species and powers from stoichiometry.

The reaction quotient Q uses the current composition. If Q<K, net forward reaction is favoured until equilibrium is approached; if Q>K, the net direction is reverse. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the usual expression because their activities are effectively constant.

workedExample.prompt: For A⇌2B, Kc=4. At [A]=0.50 M and [B]=1.0 M, predict net direction.
steps: Since Qc<Kc, the reaction proceeds net forward to produce more B.

misconception.claim: Equilibrium means reactant and product concentrations are equal.
misconception.correction: It means opposing rates are equal; concentrations obey K and can differ greatly.

questions.prompt: For the same reaction, [A]=0.25 M and [B]=2 M. Find Qc and direction when Kc=4.
questions.answer: Qc=16; net reverse.

questions.prompt: Does a catalyst change K at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: No. It speeds approach to equilibrium.

questions.hint: Use the same expression for Q and K.
questions.prompt: For A⇌B, Kc=3.0. If [A]=0.20 M and [B]=0.60 M, is there a net reaction direction?
questions.answer: Q=0.60/0.20=3.0=K, so there is no net compositional change at equilibrium, although both directions continue.
checkpoints: Calculate Q=3.0 and compare with K.
Distinguish no net change from stopped reactions.
hints: Use the same expression for Q and K.
Compare rates rather than imagining molecules become inactive.

questions.hint: Track the exponent on every concentration.
questions.prompt: For N₂(g)+3H₂(g)⇌2NH₃(g), a mixture is initially at equilibrium at fixed temperature. Its volume is suddenly halved. Using Q, predict the net direction immediately after compression.
questions.answer: Every gas concentration doubles, so Q changes by 2²/(2×2³)=1/4. Starting at equilibrium, Q becomes K/4 and the net reaction forms NH₃.
checkpoints: Apply doubling to all gas concentrations.
hints: Track the exponent on every concentration.
The numerator has total exponent two and the denominator four.

notes.title: Reasoning through equilibrium quotients and reaction direction
paragraphs: An equilibrium constant is written for one balanced reaction at a specified temperature. The reaction quotient uses the same expression with current activities or, in the usual classroom approximation, concentrations. Comparing Q with K predicts the direction of net change, not an instantaneous halt of molecular reactions. Pure solids and liquids are omitted from the expression because their activities are approximately constant. Changing concentration or pressure can alter Q and cause redistribution; changing temperature can alter K. A catalyst speeds both directions towards equilibrium without changing its composition at the same temperature.

workedExamples.prompt: For H₂+I₂⇌2HI, Kc=4.0. Initially [H₂]=[I₂]=1.0 M and [HI]=0. Find the equilibrium concentrations.
steps: Let x M of each reactant be consumed. Then [HI]=2x and [H₂]=[I₂]=1−x.
Set 4=(2x)²/(1−x)². Taking the positive root gives 2=2x/(1−x), so x=0.50.
workedExamples.conclusion: Equilibrium concentrations are 0.50 M H₂, 0.50 M I₂ and 1.0 M HI.

flashcards.front: What does Q<K predict?
flashcards.back: Net forward reaction towards products.

flashcards.front: Are reactions stopped at equilibrium?
flashcards.back: No; forward and reverse rates are equal.

flashcards.front: What changes K for a fixed reaction?
flashcards.back: Temperature.

flashcards.front: Why omit a pure solid from K?
flashcards.back: Its activity is approximately constant in the equilibrium model.

modules.title: Acids, bases and buffer ratios
modules.focus: Use equilibrium rather than treating every acid as fully dissociated.
explanation: A strong acid dissociates essentially completely in dilute aqueous solution, while a weak acid establishes an equilibrium. pH=-log₁₀[H₃O⁺] in the usual concentration approximation. A tenfold concentration change shifts pH by one unit.

A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in appreciable amounts. The Henderson-Hasselbalch relation pH=pKa+log([base]/[acid]) explains its ratio dependence. Buffer capacity is finite and depends on amounts, not only the ratio.

workedExample.prompt: A buffer has pKa=4.8 and equal concentrations of acid and conjugate base. Find pH.
steps: The base-to-acid ratio is 1, whose logarithm is zero.
The calculated pH is 4.8.

misconception.claim: A buffer prevents every pH change regardless of acid added.
misconception.correction: It resists limited additions until its reactive components are substantially consumed.

questions.prompt: Find the pH of an ideal dilute solution with [H₃O⁺]=1.0×10⁻³ M.
For pKa=5 and [base]/[acid]=10, find buffer pH.
checkpoints: More conjugate base raises pH above pKa.

questions.hint: A ratio below one has a negative logarithm.
questions.prompt: A buffer has pKa=6.0 and [A⁻]/[HA]=0.10. Calculate pH and identify the more abundant member.
questions.answer: pH=6.0+log(0.10)=5.0; HA is ten times more abundant than A⁻.
checkpoints: Identify HA as the more abundant member.
hints: A ratio below one has a negative logarithm.
Interpret the ratio as base divided by acid.

questions.prompt: Compare a buffer containing 0.010 mol each of HA and A⁻ with one containing 0.10 mol each in the same volume. Which better resists a fixed small acid addition, and why?
questions.answer: Their initial pH values are approximately equal because the ratios match. The second has greater capacity because it contains ten times as much A⁻ to consume added acid.
checkpoints: Recognise equal initial ratios and approximate pH.
Connect greater amount to smaller fractional change during acid addition.
hints: Separate ratio from total amount.
Ask what fraction of the base a fixed addition consumes.

notes.title: Reasoning through acids, bases and buffer ratios
paragraphs: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one proton. Strong acids in the dilute classroom model ionise essentially completely, while weak acids require an equilibrium calculation. A buffer contains appreciable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base; it consumes small added amounts of acid or base by reaction. For such additions, perform the stoichiometric reaction first, then use the new ratio in the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation when its approximations remain reasonable. Dilution approximately preserves this ratio and hence pH, but lowers the total amount available to resist further additions. Buffer capacity is therefore distinct from buffer pH.

workedExamples.prompt: A buffer contains 0.20 mol HA and 0.30 mol A⁻ with pKa=5.0. Add 0.10 mol strong acid without significant volume change. Find the new pH.
steps: Added H⁺ consumes A⁻ and produces HA: amounts become 0.20 mol A⁻ and 0.30 mol HA.
workedExamples.conclusion: The new buffer pH is about 4.82.

flashcards.front: What changes between conjugate partners?
flashcards.back: One proton.

flashcards.front: What should precede a buffer-equilibrium calculation after strong acid addition?
flashcards.back: Stoichiometric consumption of the added acid.

flashcards.front: At pH=pKa, what is the buffer ratio?
Does unchanged buffer pH imply unchanged capacity?
flashcards.back: No; dilution reduces capacity while approximately preserving the ratio.

modules.title: Free energy and electrochemical driving force
modules.focus: Connect thermodynamic favourability with cell potential.
explanation: At constant temperature and pressure, negative reaction Gibbs free-energy change indicates thermodynamic favourability in the stated direction. ΔG=ΔH-TΔS requires consistent units and temperature in kelvin. Favourability does not establish that the reaction occurs quickly.

For a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The relation ΔG°=-nFE° connects standard free energy with standard cell potential. Electrons travel through the external circuit; ions move in the electrolyte to preserve charge balance.

workedExample.prompt: For ΔH=-40 kJ/mol and ΔS=-0.100 kJ/(mol K), calculate ΔG at 300 K.
steps: ΔG=-40-(-30)=-10 kJ/mol, so the reaction is favourable under these stated conditions.

misconception.claim: A favourable reaction must happen rapidly.
misconception.correction: Kinetics and activation barriers determine rate independently of the sign of ΔG.

questions.prompt: For n=2, E°=1.0 V and F=96,485 C/mol, calculate ΔG°.
questions.answer: -192,970 J/mol, approximately -193 kJ/mol.

questions.prompt: At which electrode does oxidation occur in a galvanic cell?
questions.hint: Use the reaction definition of anode.
questions.answer: At the anode.
checkpoints: Electrons leave the anode through the circuit.

questions.prompt: A process has ΔH=+30 kJ/mol and ΔS=+0.100 kJ/(mol K). At what temperature is ΔG=0, and on which side is ΔG negative?
questions.answer: T=30/0.100=300 K. Above 300 K, TΔS exceeds ΔH and ΔG is negative, assuming ΔH and ΔS remain approximately constant.
checkpoints: Identify the higher-temperature favourable side with the approximation.
hints: Solve for the equality temperature.
Evaluate the sign of ΔH−TΔS above it.

questions.hint: Use the free-energy relation to interpret E.
questions.prompt: A galvanic cell has positive E under operating conditions, but its current decreases as reactants are consumed. Does positive E prove a fixed current? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Positive E indicates thermodynamic driving force; current also depends on kinetics, resistance and transport, which can change as the cell operates.
checkpoints: Connect positive E with negative ΔG.
Identify a kinetic, resistance or transport limitation.
hints: Use the free-energy relation to interpret E.
Consider factors that control charge-flow rate.

notes.title: Reasoning through free energy and electrochemical driving force
paragraphs: Thermodynamic favourability describes the sign of Gibbs free energy under specified conditions, not how quickly a reaction proceeds. Use consistent energy units in ΔG=ΔH−TΔS and temperature in kelvin. A galvanic cell has positive cell potential for its spontaneous forward process, related to negative Gibbs free energy by ΔG=−nFE. Standard quantities refer to standard states; changing concentrations can change the actual driving force. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells, even though electrode signs differ between those cell types.

workedExamples.prompt: A galvanic cell uses standard reduction potentials +0.80 V and −0.40 V with two transferred electrons. Find E°cell and ΔG°, taking F=96,500 C/mol.
steps: The more positive reduction potential is the cathode. E°cell=0.80−(−0.40)=1.20 V.
workedExamples.conclusion: The standard cell potential is 1.20 V and ΔG° is approximately −232 kJ/mol.

flashcards.front: What does ΔG<0 establish?
flashcards.back: Thermodynamic favourability in the stated direction and conditions.

flashcards.front: Does ΔG<0 guarantee a fast reaction?
flashcards.back: No; an activation barrier can make it slow.

flashcards.front: Where does oxidation occur?
flashcards.back: At the anode.

flashcards.front: Why must T be in kelvin?
flashcards.back: The thermodynamic temperature scale is required in TΔS.
